newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Northern NZ battens down hatches as Fergus arrives.
newsitem.headline: Northern NZ battens down hatches as Fergus arrives.

text.p: Inhabitants of northern New Zealand towns battened down the hatches on Monday, preparing to farewell the year with a hiss and a roar as the remains of Cyclone Fergus bore down on the country.
Fergus is a former tropical cyclone which originated in New Caledonia and is spreading south down New Zealand.
The Meterological Service said it now classed Fergus as a "very deep depression" but people should not be fooled by the downgrade, as the impact on land would be almost as intense.

Winds are expected to gust as high as 110 km/hour (70 miles/hour) in exposed places, and Auckland region Civil Defence spokesman Graham McKean said they may lift roofs and uproot trees. He said it was possible Fergus would close Auckland's northwestern motorway and Harbour Bridge, with flooding likely throughout the region.
Civil Defence was meeting with police and fire services to formulate contingency plans.

"The problem is we've got the high tide coming up around about 12 o'clock, and if the wind coincides with that there could be a few problems -- we're hoping they both won't be in the same place at the same time," McKean said.
More than 280 millimetres (11 inches) of rain have fallen in the last 24 hours in some northern regions.
MetService forecaster Augie Auer told Radio New Zealand that some rivers could be flooded in an hour when the full force of the storm hits, because the ground is saturated from rain.
"Response time is next to nothing. It could be four hours on a good day, but as wet as everything is now, the rivers could come up in a matter of probably an hour or less," he said.

Holidaymakers on Sunday night packed up and left camping grounds throughout the North Island. In the town of Kerikeri, 1,500 Youth for Christ campers went home, and in the Hunua Ranges, southeast of Auckland, 140 children and 60 adults were evacuated from another camp.

Ports and marinas were packed as trawlers, commercial boats and yachts took refuge before the storm struck. But sailors in a round-the-world race were reported to be unconcerned about Fergus, saying the conditions would be nothing new.

The first of the 14 yachts in the BT Global Challenge was expected to enter Wellington harbour later in the day. The yachts have been sailing for 40 days from Rio de Janeiro on the second leg of their round-the-world voyage.
